name: watcher
title: The Watcher: Tell Me When It Offers Merge
part: The release, in the order it runs
html:
The Watcher: Tell Me When It Offers Merge

Ask Once

watcher:watch: this resource, the relation scm:merge, and a reply form to answer on.

It Looks, as HEART

Every 3 seconds: does the pull request’s answer offer scm:merge now?

Be Told Later

completed, signed, when it does. failed, not offered in time, when it never does.

It doesn’t know what a pull request is. It knows what an offer is.

From the kept script 
- enter: ${watcher}
  steps:
    - ask: watcher:watch
      fields:
        resource: ${pr.@self}
        offers: scm:merge
      reply: watch
- once-answered:
    reply: watch
    steps:
      - enter: ${pr.@self}
        steps:
          - act: scm:merge
            fields:
              method: squash
say: Is it ready to merge yet? The usual answer is a polling loop, written for one service, checking one field. We asked a different question: tell me when this pull request offers the merge act. The offer watcher is a small RISE service, and it speaks HEART like everything else. ARTIE asks it, with the pull request's address, the relation scm:merge, and a reply form of its own to be answered on. Then ARTIE stops waiting. Every three seconds the watcher reads the pull request: does its answer offer merge now? The moment it does, the watcher answers ARTIE's reply, signed, and ARTIE merges, by squashing, and checks it really is merged. Notice that the watcher doesn't know what a pull request is. It knows what an offer is. Next: build it.

deck:ref.name: rise
deck:ref.label: RISE
deck:ref.title: RISE: tell me when it's done
deck:ref.summary: Reciprocal Interface for State Exchange. Replies for asynchronous work: ask now, be told later. A watcher or a build answers back when it is ready, as Jenkins does in the release.

deck:ref.name: hypertext
deck:ref.label: HYPERTEXT
deck:ref.title: What hypertext means
deck:ref.summary: His definition: information and controls, presented together. Machines can follow links too.
deck:ref.quote:
“When I say hypertext, I mean the simultaneous presentation of information and controls such that the information becomes the affordance through which the user (or automaton) obtains choices and selects actions. Hypermedia is just an expansion on what text means to include temporal anchors within a media stream; most researchers have dropped the distinction.

Hypertext does not need to be HTML on a browser. Machines can follow links when they understand the data format and relationship types.”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, comment on “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”
